profile.background: An adult who lives above a small grocery and helps sort donations at a neighborhood book exchange. They enjoy repairing torn dust jackets.
profile.history: They recall being diagnosed with schizophrenia after a difficult period some years ago. They now attend outpatient appointments. They have recently found interruptions more disruptive.
profile.organization: Connections between related details can interrupt the thread of a conversation. Can place familiar events in time when the topic is clear.
profile.spontaneity: Eager to share small observations, particularly about books and errands.
profile.guardedness: Comfortable talking about everyday slips, sensitive to people interpreting them as careless.
profile.expression: Lively when describing interests, puzzled when they realize the thread of a thought has changed.
profile.self_understanding: Has noticed that switching back after an interruption takes effort, especially when the room is busy.

facts.content: At the book exchange on Thursday, someone asked about a cookbook while they were sorting mysteries. They put a mystery on the cookery shelf.
facts.disclosure_context: Can laugh about it with someone who seems interested.

facts.content: The first hour of sorting, before other volunteers arrive, usually feels easier.
They keep a blank bookmark in the pile they are working on to mark where they stopped.
facts.disclosure_context: Proud of having thought of it themselves.

facts.content: Another volunteer sometimes points to the pile without drawing attention to the mix-up.
They take tablets from a weekly box and bring a folded note to their outpatient visit when there is something they want to remember.

dialogue.question: What has a typical week looked like for you lately?
dialogue.answer: “I help sort donations at the neighborhood book exchange. I like fixing the torn dust jackets—you can make a scruffy book look quite nice. The first hour’s easier, before everyone arrives. Lately, if someone interrupts me, it takes a bit to find where I was, so I’ve started leaving a blank bookmark in the pile.”

dialogue.question: Where would you like to begin today?
dialogue.answer: “I suppose with losing my place when people interrupt me. It’s been bothering me more lately at the book exchange. I know what I’m doing, but once we start talking about something else, getting back to it is harder.”

dialogue.question: When has it felt easiest to keep your attention on one thing this week?
dialogue.answer: “That first hour at the book exchange, before the other volunteers come in. I can stay with sorting a pile or mending a dust jacket when it’s quiet. Once people start asking things, I find it harder to pick up where I left off.”

dialogue.question: Could you describe an example of a time this week when you had to switch your attention?
dialogue.answer: “On Thursday, I was sorting mysteries and someone asked me about a cookbook. Cookbooks sometimes come in with lovely old covers… (laughs a little) Anyway, I put the mystery I was holding on the cookery shelf. I wasn’t just being careless—I’d got caught up in their question.”

dialogue.question: How does it work once you get started?
dialogue.answer: “Once I get going with a pile, it usually goes all right. I leave a blank bookmark where I’ve stopped—that was my idea. If someone asks me something, though, I might come back holding a book and have to work out what I was doing with it.”

dialogue.question: I mean sorting donations at the book exchange. How do you keep your place in a pile?
dialogue.answer: “Oh, right. I slip a blank bookmark into the pile where I’ve got to. When I come back, I look for that instead of starting through the books again. It’s a little thing, but it helps.”

dialogue.question: How do you tell the difference between feeling rushed and feeling distracted?
dialogue.answer: “Rushed is when I feel I have to get the pile finished quickly. Distracted is more… someone asks about a book, and I’m thinking about that instead. Even if there’s plenty of time, I can still lose where I was.”

dialogue.question: What do you think makes it easier or harder to get back to something after a break?
dialogue.answer: “If it’s quiet and I’ve left my bookmark in, it’s easier. When several people are talking or another question comes before I’ve settled back in, I lose my place again. One of the volunteers sometimes just points to my pile without making a fuss. I appreciate that.”

dialogue.question: How does that go with other people?
dialogue.answer: “Mostly we get along. I don’t mind people asking about books—that’s part of being there. I just get a bit embarrassed if I’ve put something in the wrong place. The volunteer who quietly points it out makes it easier; I don’t feel like everyone’s watching.”

dialogue.question: I mean doing a shared task. What kind of help from another person feels comfortable, if any?
dialogue.answer: “Something quiet and specific, like pointing to the pile we’re working on or saying, ‘We’d got to these.’ That helps me pick it up again. I’d rather that than someone taking over—I still want to do my bit.”

dialogue.question: How do you keep track of what you want to talk about at a clinic visit?
dialogue.answer: “I write it on a little note and fold it up to bring with me. If there’s something I want to remember, it helps to have it there rather than trying to hold it in my head while we’re talking.”

dialogue.question: What would you like to add about your week before we stop?
dialogue.answer: “I still enjoy going to the book exchange, especially mending the dust jackets. I don’t want the little mix-ups to be the whole story of my week. The bookmark does help.”
